newsitem.title: GABON: British troops wait in the sun for Zaire action.
newsitem.headline: British troops wait in the sun for Zaire action.

text.p: British troops sprawled around a hotel pool in Gabon on Saturday as frantic diplomacy tried to ensure their possible mission to evacuate Britons from Zaire would be unnecessary.

"We've just been soaking up the sun since we got here," said one sergeant from Belfast in Northern Ireland, who preferred to keep his identity secret. He had already served abroad in Somalia and Bosnia.
Gabon, a densely forested country on Central Africa's Atlantic coast, is the rear support base for British evacuation plans for Zaire's capital Kinshasa.

Laurent Kabila's rebels have threatened to storm the teeming city of five million, also home to thousands of Western nationals including dozens of Britons, if President Mobutu Sese Seko does not hand over power.

South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki met Mobutu in Gabon's capital Libreville on Saturday to invite him to talks with Kabila which might avert a feared bloodbath in Kinshasa. Mbeki later said Mobutu and Kabila had agreed to meet on Wednesday.
"We are basically supporting British troops forward in Brazzaville," Royal Air Force Wing Commander Peter Williams told Reuters. He commands the British troops in Gabon.
"The basic mission is evacuation of British nationals...it is not a peacekeeping mission," said Williams of the RAF 70 squadron based at Lyneham in Wiltshire.

The bulk of the British evacuation force is based in Brazzaville, the capital of Congo, only three km (two miles) across the Zaire River from Kinshasa waiting for the order to go in if trouble breaks out.
Williams said that including his own fighting men the British force numbers around 500.
Also in Brazzaville are troops from the United States, and Zaire's former colonial rulers Belgium, France and Portugal.

Hundreds of people were killed in Kinshasa when Mobutu's ragged army went on the rampage in 1991 and 1993. Residents are appalled at the thought they may do the same again if they face defeat at the hands of the rebels.

Mobutu has dominated Zaire for over three decades, but his hold has been broken over the sprawling state at the heart of Africa by the rebellion which began in October. He is also suffering from prostate cancer.
Of several thousand European and North American expatriates in Kinshasa most are Belgian or French.
In Libreville some British troops are stationed with a French infantry battalion, others are billeted in a four-star hotel.
British soldiers and airmen, a rare sight in the former French colony, say they spend their time preparing to go into action.
"It is an alien climate," said Williams. "But the men are adjusting."
Troops have to drink copious amounts of water and adjust to temperatures of 90 degrees Fahrenheit (32 Celsius) in the shade and 95 percent humidity.
All complain that their most difficult battle so far has been with the local telephone system as they try to get through to loved ones at home in Britain.
"We just hope it will blow over and all turn out well for the Zaireans," one sergeant said from his deck chair.
